section_summary: This section combines reports on Japanese Army leadership changes, national-defense mobilization, military industry, anti-foreign controls, and proposed legislation protecting military-resource secrets. It includes biographical intelligence on senior generals, diplomatic and attaché reporting from 1937–1939, and administrative cross-reference sheets. The largest subfile is the opening portion of a March 1939 U.S. Army combat estimate detailing Japan’s defense command, manpower, field organization, weapons, aviation, logistics, and reserve forces.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Shifts in the Japanese Mukden Command
subfiles.about: A filing note summarizes and cross-references a telegram reporting imminent changes in the Japanese high command at Mukden.
subfiles.summary: The note states that changes in the Japanese Mukden command were expected shortly. It interprets General Ishiwara's removal as evidence of détente with Russia and a concentration of Japanese effort in China, and directs the reader to the attached telegram.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 436: Japanese Command Changes at Mukden
subfiles.about: Salisbury forwards a Mukden report forecasting transfers and replacements among the senior commanders of the Kwantung Army.
subfiles.summary: The report says Commander-in-Chief and Ambassador Ueda would be transferred to an advisory office in Tokyo and replaced by General Terauchi, whose place would be taken by General Doihara. General Ishiwara, Vice Chief of Staff of the Kwantung Army, was also expected to be relieved. His removal was interpreted as a move away from conflict with Russia and toward concentrating Japanese efforts in China.

subfiles.title: Who's Who in the Army: Lieutenant General Hideki Tojo
subfiles.about: A biographical intelligence report traces Hideki Tojo's military career and assesses his appointment as Vice Minister of War.
subfiles.summary: The report supplies a chronological service record culminating in Tojo's leadership in the Kwantung Army and appointment as Vice Minister of War. It links the appointment to the May 1938 cabinet reorganization and the selection of officers aligned with the conduct of operations in China. Tojo is characterized as able and generally approved within the Army.

subfiles.title: Who's Who in National Defense: Lieutenant General Seishirō Itagaki
subfiles.from: Harry I. T. Creswell, Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The report reviews Seishirō Itagaki's career and evaluates his appointment as Japan's Minister of War.
subfiles.summary: Itagaki's record includes service in the Russo-Japanese War, duty in China and Manchuria, senior posts in the Kwantung Army, and command of the 5th Division. His June 1938 appointment as Minister of War is treated as notable because many officers were senior to him. The report describes him as able, knowledgeable about China and Manchuria, popular among commissioned personnel, and likely to favor aggressive operations in China.

subfiles.title: Who's Who in the Army: Lieutenant General Masao Kishimoto
subfiles.from: Harry I. T. Creswell, Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.about: A personnel report outlines the artillery career of Lieutenant General Masao Kishimoto.
subfiles.summary: The report follows Kishimoto from his commissioning in 1904 through artillery regimental, instructional, and school commands to his appointment as Inspector General of Artillery in 1938. It describes him as one of the artillery branch's foremost officers. It also notes that he attained general-officer rank without attending the Staff College.

subfiles.title: Observations in Relation to Matters of Possible Military Interest: Nagasaki Consular District
subfiles.about: Bruner reports on defense-related industrial expansion, civil mobilization, and growing restrictions on foreigners in the Nagasaki consular district.
subfiles.summary: The report describes oil storage, fortifications, steel and chemical production, a reported poison-gas plant near Moji, naval activity at Sasebo, and Mitsubishi industrial expansion around Nagasaki Bay. It examines propaganda, military training, air-raid drills, troop send-offs, and commemorative rituals used to create public solidarity around national defense. Bruner also reports heightened surveillance and harassment of foreigners, missionary withdrawals from the Ryukyus and southern Kyushu, and attributes much of the regional anti-foreign campaign to the gendarmerie commandant at Kumamoto.

subfiles.title: Confidential Memorandum on Japanese Army and Government Changes in China
subfiles.about: The memorandum reports anticipated Japanese command changes and renewed pressure on Wu Peifu to lead a Japanese-sponsored government in China.
subfiles.summary: A Peiping source believed Kuniaki Koiso, commander of Japanese forces in Korea, would replace Terauchi and pursue a more active North China policy. The change was expected to strengthen Kwantung Army control in Tokyo and across Japanese-occupied China. The memorandum also says Wu Peifu's resistance to replacing Wang Kemin was weakening, while Doihara was mentioned as a less likely alternative.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: National Mobilization in Japan
subfiles.about: A cross-reference points to Ambassador Grew's despatch No. 3380 and its enclosed memorandum on Japanese national mobilization.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers the reader to despatch No. 3380 from Japan, dated November 1, 1938. That despatch enclosed a memorandum prepared by Max W. Schmidt concerning national mobilization in Japan.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Further Implementation of the National General Mobilization Law
subfiles.about: A cross-reference directs readers to Grew's despatch No. 3640 concerning an ordinance implementing Japan's National General Mobilization Law.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies a January 30, 1939 despatch from Japan on further implementation of the National General Mobilization Law. The referenced despatch enclosed a translation of Imperial Ordinance No. 5, promulgated January 6, 1939, together with an appendix.

subfiles.title: Departmental Note on Proposed Legislation to Suppress Industrial Espionage
subfiles.about: The note summarizes Tokyo despatch No. 3714 and warns that Japan's proposed military-resource secrecy law could impede American commercial reporting.
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs characterizes the proposed legislation as exceptionally broad, covering materials that possessed or might later acquire military significance. It predicts that enactment would seriously handicap American consulates and other government representatives seeking commercial information in Japan.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3714: Proposed Legislation to Suppress Industrial Espionage
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew reports on a proposed Japanese law intended to preserve secrecy concerning a sweeping range of military resources.
subfiles.summary: The despatch lists fifteen categories of protected information, including war-production capacity, strategic stocks and imports, technicians, aircraft, vehicles, horses, railways, airports, ships, communications, research, weather, and concealed installations. War and Navy ministers would receive broad powers to demand reports, restrict access, order concealment, and prohibit disclosure. Grew concludes that strict enforcement could obstruct legitimate commercial information gathering and promises a translation after passage and promulgation.

subfiles.title: Attaché's Report No. 44: Japanese Military Police
subfiles.to: Office of the Chief of Naval Operations, Navy Department
subfiles.about: The Naval Attaché analyzes three foreign-policy questions that Japanese military police reportedly sought to have him answer.
subfiles.summary: The military police wanted opinions on the duration of the China war, the United States reaction to the occupation of Hainan, and whether Russia would attack Japan during a European war. The report treats the questions as possible evidence of uncertainty about China, concern over the diplomatic consequences of Japan's southward expansion, and limited knowledge of Soviet intentions. It also considers possible German-Italian-Japanese military understandings and cites William Henry Chamberlin's views on the improbability of a Japanese-Soviet war.

subfiles.title: G-2 Report No. 9735: Law for the Protection of Secrets Concerning Military Resources
subfiles.from: Harry I. T. Creswell, Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Creswell supplies a translation and assessment of Japan's proposed law protecting secrets connected with military resources.
subfiles.summary: The translated draft defines protected information broadly, covering industrial output and capacity, stockpiles, imports, technical personnel, transport, aviation, shipping, communications, research, weather, and concealed facilities. It authorizes ministers to designate secrets, mark documents, conceal installations, restrict entry and observation, control official records, conduct inspections, and compensate affected owners. Severe penalties apply to espionage, publication, disclosure to foreigners, prohibited observation, false reporting, and organized attempts to acquire secrets, including offenses committed outside Japan. Creswell concludes that the measure supplements the earlier Military Secrets Protection Law so comprehensively that almost any military-related information could be restricted and even the list of secrets concealed.

subfiles.title: Charge Slip: File 894.27 Enclosure
subfiles.about: An administrative charge slip records circulation or temporary removal of an enclosure associated with file 894.27.
subfiles.summary: The page contains routing abbreviations, clerks' entries, and several handwritten or stamped numbers and dates. It provides no substantive discussion of Japanese military affairs.

subfiles.title: Japan Combat Estimate
subfiles.about: The opening portion of a comprehensive U.S. military estimate describes Japan's national-defense system, Army manpower, organization, combat arms, aviation, services, and reserves.
subfiles.summary: After a detailed table of contents, the estimate explains the Emperor's supreme command and the roles of the Board of Marshals and Admirals, High Military Council, Imperial Headquarters, War Ministry, General Staff, training inspectorates, and aviation authorities. It estimates Japanese manpower and wartime deployments across Manchukuo, Korea, Taiwan, China, and the home islands, then describes heavy and proposed light divisions and the organization and equipment of infantry, armor, artillery, cavalry, engineers, signals, transport, and military police. Extensive tables cover Army Air Corps personnel, aircraft, squadron organization, bases, maintenance, and command arrangements. The surviving pages end during discussions of chemical warfare, ordnance, intendance, medical and veterinary services, and reserve manpower, with the estimate continuing beyond this section.
